scenes.title: Locks
scenes.narration: Locks are the mechanism a database uses to coordinate concurrent access so that transactions do not overwrite or misread each other's data.

scenes.title: Shared versus exclusive locks

left.title: Shared (read) lock
points: Many transactions can hold it on the same row at once

right.title: Exclusive (write) lock
points: Only one transaction can hold it on a row
Blocks all other shared and exclusive locks

scenes.narration: There are two fundamental lock modes. A shared lock is taken to read data, and many transactions can hold shared locks on the same row simultaneously because reads do not conflict. An exclusive lock is taken to modify data, and only one transaction can hold it on a given row. An exclusive lock is incompatible with every other lock, so it blocks any reader or writer trying to touch the same row.

scenes.title: Lock granularity
bullets: Row-level locks: fine-grained, allow high concurrency on the same table
Table-level locks: coarse, simple but block the whole table
Finer granularity means more concurrency but more locks to manage
The engine may escalate many row locks into a table lock
scenes.narration: Locks come at different granularities. Row-level locks are fine-grained, letting many transactions work on different rows of the same table at once for high concurrency. Table-level locks are coarse and simple but block everyone from the whole table. Finer locks allow more parallelism but cost more overhead to track, and some engines escalate a flood of row locks into a single table lock.

scenes.title: Acquiring row locks with FOR UPDATE
scenes.narration: SELECT FOR UPDATE explicitly acquires an exclusive lock on the rows it reads. Here we lock account one at the start of the transaction. Any other transaction that tries to lock or modify that same row will now block and wait until we finish. We safely compute and apply the new balance, then COMMIT, which releases the lock and lets the waiting transactions proceed. This pattern prevents lost updates when two clients read-modify-write the same row.

scenes.title: How blocking happens
steps: Transaction A takes an exclusive lock on a row
Transaction B requests an incompatible lock on that row
B is blocked and waits in a queue
When A commits or rolls back, its locks release and B proceeds
scenes.narration: Blocking is the natural consequence of incompatible locks. When transaction A holds an exclusive lock on a row and transaction B asks for an incompatible lock on the same row, B cannot proceed and is placed in a wait queue. Only when A ends by committing or rolling back are its locks released, at which point B is unblocked and continues. Keeping transactions short minimizes how long others wait.

scenes.text: Hold locks for as short a time as possible: keep transactions brief and commit promptly so you do not block other work and hurt overall throughput.
scenes.narration: The practical takeaway is to hold locks for as little time as possible. Keep transactions brief and commit promptly so you release locks quickly and avoid blocking other work.
